title: We Asked 17 Sommeliers: What’s the One Wine You Always Order When You See It on a Menu?
summary:

content:
Exploration is one of wine’s greatest virtues. A bottle shop or wine menu can take you from the Rheinessen’s steep hills to the peaks of Mendoza to the sea salt-dusted cliffs of the San Luis Obispo Coast. Even within a single region, drinkers can taste a world of grapes, terroirs, and climates.

That said, there are some wines that are far too special to pass up. Coming across one of these bottles can warrant a repeat order — exploring the wine world’s vast offerings can pick back up tomorrow. Wines that fall under the must-order category might be small production, highly allocated bottles that don’t pop up too frequently. Even the experts — who are constantly learning about and tasting dozens of new wines each day — have the coveted bottles and producers that they can’t help but order when the opportunity presents itself.

That’s why we asked 17 sommeliers to name the wines they just can’t resist when perusing a list. From small producers in California to specific vintages of Cru Beaujolais, here’s what they said.

The wines sommeliers must order if they see it on a menu:

  • Lady of the Sunshine Chene Vineyard Pinot Noir
  • Les Jardins de la Martinière ‘Shi Ro’ 2018
  • Antinori Tignanello
  • Cinsault from Bechthold Vineyard in Lodi, Calif.
  • Cool-climate Syrah
  • Jonata ‘La Sangre de Jonata’ Syrah
  • Domaine Alice et Olivier de Moor Bourgogne Aligoté Plantation 1902
  • Alain Castex
  • Valentini Cerasuolo d’Abruzzo
  • Mac Forbes
  • Collecapretta ‘Terra dei Preti’
  • Stein Palmberg Alte Reben Riesling Kabinett Trocken 2021
  • Sette Grignolino Piemonte
  • Elio Sandri Barolo ‘Perno’ 2020
  • Jean Foillard ‘Côte du Py’ Morgon 2017
  • Tortona Timorasso
  • Domaine du Collier
  • Occidental Pinot Noir Freestone-Occidental 2024

“My answer is any of the Lady of the Sunshine wines, but my favorite is the Lady of the Sunshine Chene Vineyard Pinot Noir. Not only do I love the wine, but I’m also a fan of the winemaker and owner, Gina Giugni. She and her husband have a more recognized label called Scar of the Sea, but Lady of the Sunshine is her solo project. The messaging behind their production is ‘a love letter to the Central Coast’ in California. Gina is a second generation biodynamic farmer. She is such a thoughtful producer of low intervention wine, and that care really shows up in the bottle. The Pinot Noir is elegant and soft, which I expect and seek from Pinots, but there is an edge of grit that expresses through minerality and a playful nose of strawberry hard candies. There is also a scarcity of the product as they only produce a few hundred cases of each of their wines. I always want to reward restaurants for carrying her wines and enjoy a glass myself!” —Leah Matthews, Daisies and The Radicle, Chicago

“Les Jardins de la Martinière ‘Shi Ro’ 2018: less than a hectare of Chenin vines goes into this. It’s spellbinding and very hard to find. Kaya Tsutsui and Hirotake Ooka are clearly so talented, and their first vintage (2018) was only released a few years ago.” —Grace Rogers, head sommelier, Stars, New York City

“If I spot Antinori Tignanello on a wine list, it’s always a bottle worth considering. Tignanello helped redefine Italian winemaking, challenging tradition while remaining deeply connected to its Tuscan roots. It is so special because of its beautiful balance between dark fruit, savory complexity, refined tannins, and vibrant acidity. It’s powerful without being overwhelming and elegant without sacrificing character. A truly memorable wine should tell a story, and Tignanello does exactly that. It’s a remarkable expression of craftsmanship, innovation, and the extraordinary potential of Tuscany.” —Scott Jones, sommelier, The Edge Steakhouse at The Ritz-Carlton, Rancho Mirage, Greater Palm Springs, Calif.

“Not a single bottle, but a single vineyard. Cinsault from Bechtold Vineyard in Lodi. It’s home to 135-year-old vines, which is just crazy to think about in California. The oldest own-rooted Cinsault in the world. I’ve had three bottlings from three producers: Two Shepherds, Time Place, and Turley. All three take a very hands-off approach and let the vineyard tell the story. You get incredible aromatics of plum and purple flowers, delicate body and spice, and a long finish with great acid. Gamay and Pinot Noir are good entry points, but this is like nothing else in California.” —Scott Stroemer, Galit and Cafe Yaya, NYC

“I don’t know if I have a wine I always order, but Syrah comes pretty close to a 100-percent order for me, especially if it’s coming from a cool-climate region. While I would typically lean Northern Rhône, I have fallen into a rabbit hole of cooler, coastal Syrah from California. Jonata ‘La Sangre de Jonata’ Syrah from Ballard Canyon is something I’ve really been enjoying recently. The savory, peppery qualities are beautiful, and while there are tannins, they aren’t as aggressive as that of Cabernet.” —Alex Cuper, wine director, El Che and Brasero, Chicago

“For a long time, one ‘must-order’ bottle for me has been the Plantation 1902 bottling of Aligoté from Alice and Olivier De Moor. It has the freshness and acidity that I love in Aligoté, but the fruit from the old vines gives a real depth and concentration that makes it a compelling and delicious wine.” —Max Mackinnon, co-owner, Plus de Vin, Brooklyn

“Wines from Alain Castex have been high up on my ‘if I see it, I drink it’ list since his U.S. importer, Josh Eubank, shared them with me back in 2018. His ‘Tir à Blanc,’ a sun-filled, aromatic blend of every white varietal in his Banyuls vineyards, makes me sentimental for the platonic ideal of summer on the coast of southern France, a place and time I’ve only experienced through the wines. Alain’s passing a few years ago only made my thirst and sentimentality more acute. Collectors have gone nuts for these, so if you see Vins du Cabanon or (even more uncommon) a pre-2015 Casot de Mailloles, don’t hesitate.” —Kae Whalen, wine director, Little Fish, Los Angeles

“Valentini Cerasuolo d’Abruzzo is a must order. It’s not a wine I see too often on a list so it feels like an Easter egg when I find one. It’s a serious rosé that balances aromatics, structure, and intensity in a way that feels unlike anything else. A wine that deserves a place by the pool as much as it does at the dinner table.” —Chris Gellein, wine director, Claud, NYC

“Anything from Mac Forbes in the Yarra Valley. I met Mac on a trip to Australia and fell in love with how thoughtful and site-driven his wines are. They’re elegant and full of energy, and I don’t see them on many lists, so when I do, I always order one.” —Benjamin Chesna, beverage director, Himmel Hospitality Group, Boston

“My choice is ‘Terra dei Preti’ from Collecapretta in Umbria. This is a really special cuvée that I think expresses the special winemaking and farming at Collecapretta as well as the specific grapes they have here. Every time I share this wine with a wine professional or anyone else, they are knocked out by it. It’s a wine that makes you pause, and you never want the bottle to end. It is technically an orange wine, but think of it more as a full expression of incredible Trebbiano grapes. With their wines I always want to drink one year after they arrive, which is one year after harvest. So right now I would look for something ideally from 2024 or older.” —Mike Fadem, owner, Ops, Brooklyn

“From a truly obsessive person who has had many phases of fixation in life — ask me about Weezer — the first producer I think of is Dr. Ulli Stein in the Mosel. If I ever see his Palmberg Alte Reben Kabinett Trocken 2021 on a list, it’s a no-brainer order for me. The acid from this vintage is especially drool-worthy, but there’s so much more happening, such as the touches of flinty reduction, the treasure trove of baking spices, and a prickly but friendly texture that causes such a strong knee-jerk reaction whenever I see this wine on a list.” —Haran McElroy, wine director, Smithereens, NYC

“Sette, an Italian producer founded in 2017 by a dynamic duo of young owners and winemakers who are a bit avant-garde in style. I’m currently obsessed with their Grignolino, an exceptionally light red wine reminiscent of a Pinot Noir. It is radiant in the glass with tantalizing notes of ripe strawberry and fresh soil and holds an acidity that jump-starts your salivary glands. If you don’t recognize it by name, you’ll recognize it by the label with the drawing of a red sea urchin, beckoning you to grab the bottle to scrutinize it.” —Vincent McGranahan, property sommelier, The Ava Hotel Paso Robles, Paso Robles, Calif.

“I don’t want to sound redundant because I’m Italian, but whatever you can catch and drink from Elio Sandri do it. The Barolo ‘Perno’ 2020 is incredible right now! It just landed in the U.S., and in Italy, it’s been a cult wine for a while. Get some before it’s all gone.” —Oliviero Lucchetti, beverage director, Balera, Brooklyn

“Jean Foillard ‘Côte du Py’ 2017. As far as Beaujolais goes, it’s an essential reference point as one of the region’s greatest wines from one of its most dedicated vignerons. No matter how many times I taste the 2017 vintage, it never fails to win me over with its brazen simplicity and quiet poise. There is an effortless push and pull between tart and sweet. It is also one of the few wines that is universally attractive to wine lovers of every ilk, one we can all agree is worth drinking. It speaks concisely and demands very little of you, only that you pause your speculation and analysis and enjoy it for what it is.” —Ellis Srubas-Giammanco, wine director, Penny, NYC

“Timorasso. This native white grape from the hills around Tortona in southeastern Piedmont is one of the most exciting white grapes in the world right now. The quality is so consistent that I’ll confidently order almost any bottle I see. It has a bit of red-wine grip and racy acidity, making it a natural pairing with food from nearly any cuisine. Expect a full body, bright citrus, and Mediterranean herbs, as well as a Riesling-like petrol note with a few years of age. If you love dry Alsatian whites, or you’re simply an adventurous drinker, order it. Look for Vigneti Massa, La Colombera, and La Chiara, plus Langhe heavyweights Vietti, Borgogno, and Oddero, who now make it too.” —Scott Thomas, wine director, Restaurant Olivia and Dear Emilia, Denver

“If I see Domaine du Collier on a wine list, I’m almost certainly ordering it. Antoine Foucault makes some of the most compelling wines in the Loire Valley, particularly his Cabernet Francs, which manage to be simultaneously powerful and delicate, deeply savory yet remarkably elegant. His Chenin Blancs are every bit as extraordinary, and there’s a purity and sense of place to it all that I find irresistible. To be honest, these are probably the only wines that would make me flip the page away from Burgundy, and those who know me know how big that is.” —Cody Pruitt, co-owner, Capitaine and Floradora, NYC

“The 2024 Occidental-Frestone Pinot Noir from Occidental is the wine to order 100 percent of the time. It is just pure pleasure. The purity of bright fruit in this cuvée is mouthwatering and even a little salty. This wine is the pinnacle of harmony and balance all Pinot strives to achieve. It is a great reminder of why I fell in love with Pinot Noir in the first place.” —Steven Flores, head sommelier, Lei, NYC

content:
It’s generally agreed upon that the seminal moment that shoved the modern craft cocktail revival into high gear was the opening of New York’s Milk & Honey on Dec. 31, 1999. There were plenty of signs of things to come prior to its launch: Dale DeGroff’s important work at the Rainbow Room; the opening of the original Angel’s Share in 1993; the explosion of the London cocktail bar scene in the ’90s. But Milk & Honey — and its careful curation of cocktail culture channeled through the late Sasha Petraske’s efforts — was the touchstone that influenced the scene’s quantum leap into society’s collective consciousness.

Milk & Honey’s launch was perfect timing, and not just because it dragged cocktail culture out of its decades-long nadir. It essentially took its first breath at the start of the 2000s, thus giving us the most pristine starting point to track just how modern cocktails have evolved throughout the 21st century. Since we are now one-fourth through the epoch — let that sink in for a moment — it seems like an ideal time to reflect on what’s all happened since the clandestine door at 134 Eldridge St. became the portal to a grander universe.

Here, we explore 13 of the key cocktail trends that have impacted how drinks enthusiasts imbibed during the last quarter-century. In a way, they are more than mere trends. They are a reflection of an inherently curious industry that’s grown increasingly comfortable with exploration and experimentation in ways that occasionally cross-pollinate with art, history, and science. These attitudes can’t help but spark intrigue about what’s to come between now and the century’s midway point.

It can be difficult to pin down the exact moment these trends took off or faded away. Such is the nature of cocktail history. Fortunately, enough context exists for us to create a rough timeline tracing the cocktail world’s most pervasive trends, from the outrageously bombastic to the undeniably brilliant. Please enjoy below.

2000 – 2015: The Old-School Drink Revival

The craft cocktail movement took its biggest leap forward by looking backward. As the seeds of the scene began to flower in the wake of Milk & Honey’s success, bartenders across New York City (and eventually the country) began digging through long-forgotten recipe books and historic artifacts to uncover a liquid treasure trove of bygone drinks, including several pre-Prohibition delights. Old drinks were the hot new thing for a decade-plus.

By the mid-2010s, bartenders had mostly jettisoned the wax mustache and suspender look and turned their attention toward other concepts that were unfathomable at the revival’s outset. But by then, woebegone cocktails like the Sazerac, Negroni, Bee’s Knees, and Last Word had been rightfully established as timeless classics.

2007 – 2019: Fat-Washing Takes Hold

The craft cocktail scene had established a sense of permanency by 2007. However, it was time to evolve beyond historic discoveries and simple builds. The seminal East Village Bar PDT — specifically, bartender Don Lee — sparked this advancement through the science of fat-washing. Lee created his Benton’s Old Fashioned by infusing bourbon with bacon fat procured from famed chef David Chang, giving the spirit a texturally rich, slightly unctuous flavor. The inoculated bourbon, combined with a bit of maple syrup, transformed a simple drink into an otherworldly riff that blew minds and inspired bartenders to start experimenting with their own fat infusions, pushing the technique further into the cocktail consciousness.

By the mid-2010s, bartenders around the country were fat-washing drinks with a wide range of fatty and oily mediums, from duck fat to butter. The trend took a step back just before the pandemic went down, but it never really went out of favor. It just became more mainstream, similar to other infusion tactics.

2015 – Present: Smoking Guns, Flavor Blasters, and Other Gadgetry

As the 2000s drew to a close, bartenders started to swap out their suspenders for lab coats and mess around with technical and scientific doodads. Advanced gadgets like smoking guns and iSi whippers began turning heads thanks to the pioneering efforts of mad bar scientists like Eben Freeman and Dave Arnold. While the gizmos were initially regarded as fancy tools for elite programs, they became relatively common items by around 2015 or so, ready to be used by any bartender desiring to wow guests with extra sensory engagement and a little theatrical flair.

Specific contraptions have rotated in the spotlight in the years since. The flavor blaster’s ability to top drinks with smoky bubbles was quite the rage in the years surrounding the pandemic. Arnold’s own Spinzall centrifuge device allowed bartenders to deploy techniques like fat-washing and clarification with greater efficiency when it hit the market in 2017. These days, the iSi siphon has re-emerged as a ubiquitous device after years of quasi-dormancy. Cynics and old-school cocktail aficionados may dismiss these elements as mere novelties, but even if they are, there’s no denying they have staying power.

2017 – 2019: Tiny Clothespins Hug Every Glass

It used to be cool to treat cocktail glasses like laundry. Around 2017, bartenders began affixing rims with itty-bitty clothespins, with the drink’s garnished wedged in between the two objects. Reasons why varied. Some utilized the technique to prevent the garnishes from accidentally falling off the cocktail and/or into the drink. Others said it was a unique way to integrate the garnish’s aroma into the overall flavor experience. Either way, it looked like an adorable, quite literal side piece as its popularity climbed.

It didn’t take too long for the trend to lose its steam. Wooden pins gave way to cheap, plastic versions, which looked tacky and led to environmental concerns. By the time tiny clothespins started popping up at family-friendly chain restaurants, bartenders and cocktail enthusiasts had more or less turned their backs on them. They still make an appearance on occasion, but not nearly as much as they once did.

2018 – 2022: Acid-Adjusting is Liquid Gold

Not all citrus fruit is created equal from an acidity standpoint. Oranges and grapefruits may have terrific flavors, but they aren’t as tart as lemons or limes due to their low acid content. This poses a problem in cocktails, where sharp acidity goes a long way toward achieving flavor balance. This made these weaker citrus fruits somewhat of a pariah when it came to cocktail creation for decades despite their deliciousness. The solution to all this? Mimicry.

In the mid-2010s, science-minded bartenders started acid-adjusting cocktails, adding citric acid in malic acid to drinks built around fruits with low acidity. This gave the cocktail the barbed bite of a lemon or lime along with the flavors of other citrus fruit. It was alchemy that produced legitimate liquid gold. Acid-adjustment gradually shifted from cool trend to practical post-Covid bar strategy, as bars began to use the acid add-ons to reduce waste and costs in addition to boosting a drink’s balance.

2019 – Present: Coffee and Cocktails Collide

If there’s one trend in the last quarter-century that may produce a strong sense of deja vu, it’s the ongoing mashup of coffee and cocktails. After all, the Espresso Martini achieved rock star status in the ’90s, years before the resurgence of potent potables occurred. Yet when coffee cocktails made their comeback around 2019, it weirdly felt like a fresh new thing.

The reason for the vibe may or may have nothing to do with cocktails. The third-wave coffee movement spent the last quarter-century curating a culture that extends well past the rote morning cuppa joe, infusing the drink’s lexicon with terms like cold brew concentrate, single-origin, and terroir. The third wave crashed onto the public roughly around the same time as the craft cocktail revival; in a way, this gives both movements a shared sense of DNA, which could be why this fusion became popular and enduring. Either that, or it’s a nostalgia thing. The ’90s are back, baby!

2021 – 2025: Agave Drinks Beyond the Margarita

The emergence of mezcal and the increased appreciation of tequila as more than something you shoot at a dive bar set the agave market on fire at the beginning of the decade.
This boom was bound to have an effect on cocktail culture. Guests and bartenders alike became more curious about agave spirits’ possibilities within mixed drinks outside the traditional classics or simple-yet-delicious riffs. Suddenly, it was possible to see a tequila drink on a menu without it being a Margarita, a Paloma, or a similarly familiar beverage.

These newfangled agave drinks are no longer a shiny trend — just listen for how many people call for a Mezcal Negroni on your next night out — but rather a standard sight on the scene. Of course, this doesn’t mean that the Margarita somehow stopped being a banger.

2022 – 2026: Clarified Everything

Clarifying opaque liquids like milk is a technique that’s been around for centuries. It also used to be a laborious, time-consuming effort, which relegated it to niche status at best. Then Dave Arnold created the Spinzall, and clarifying via centrifuge became another tech tool bartenders could place in their arsenal. As the industry emerged from Covid, it seemed like barkeeps everywhere couldn’t wait to show off their new skill. They couldn’t wait to tell guests, either — if a drink was clarified, it was the first thing listed on its description.

We may also be witnessing the bubble burst on this trend in real time, to the point where predicting its demise by the end of the year seems like the right call: Gripes about the trend’s ubiquitousness have been around for a while, and they’ve only gotten louder in recent months. It may not look like the trend’s over based on what current cocktail menus look like, but it sure feels like it’s on life support.

2022 – 2025: Force Carbonation Bubbles Up

In a way, force carbonation seemed like an inevitable bar trend. Home carbonation systems like the SodaStream became popular in the 2010s, and the internet is chock full of instructions for building DIY carbonation kits. It’s easy to visualize bored bartenders stuck at home during Covid’s lockdown experimenting with adding bubbles to basic drinks. If such fiddling around occurred, it clearly was a success. The technique quickly became a hot post-pandemic trend for a few years, and has nicely settled into its current stage as an essential pre-batching technique.

Force carbonation became a bar mainstay because it’s much more than a neat parlor trick. The technique intensifies a cocktail’s aromatics, texture, and flavor notes. The process also helps balance a drink’s ingredients, which can also lead to more consistent cocktails. And while it’s a practical tactic, some bartenders use it to nerd out and do complicated procedures like canning, which can make unfussy drinks like a Paloma incredibly fussy.

2023 – Present: Drinkers Embrace Savory Cocktails

The modern cocktail movement’s trendy twists and turns wouldn’t have happened if guests and their palates didn’t evolve. The savory cocktail movement could very well be the peak example of this axiom. While concepts like the Dirty Martini and Bloody Mary have been around for decades, consumers really started to lean into drinks with vegetal, salty, and umami notes around 2023. It’s not only still going strong, it’s arguably the hottest trend in cocktails today.

Bartenders have also gone all-in on the savory trend, which makes perfect sense. The drinks give them free reign to open their cupboard and reach for wild ingredients that would have seen out of place during the revival’s early days. Fish sauce, tomatoes, habanero peppers, parmesan cheese, and other unorthodox foodstuffs are all fair game now. Compare that to 25 years ago, when most customers had never heard of orange bitters. We’ve come a long way.

2023 – Present: Spritzes Hit the Scene

As people eased back into society after Covid, a common narrative surfaced. People overindulged in alcohol during lockdown, had a Talking Heads-esque “My God! What have I done?” moment, and made a concerted effort to either drink less or consume lower-ABV drinks. Spritzes provided a perfect solution for these situations, and people figured this out and embraced the category wholeheartedly.

There were other reasons why spritzes ascended to stardom: Italian aperitivo culture gained a bit of a foothold as more folks started getting together in person again, and the brightly colored drinks look pretty on TikTok. Still, it’s hard to imagine spritzes taking off as they did without people needing to slow their roll. These days, the trend keeps rolling on because they’re delicious and surprisingly versatile.

2024 – Present: NA Drinks That Aren’t an Afterthought

Chatter about people drinking less was inescapable after the pandemic. It made no difference whether the conversations stemmed from Gen Z’s perceived lack of drinking habits or people taking extended post-Covid booze breaks. By 2024, it was loud and sustainable enough to compel bars to move their spirit-free cocktail options beyond the realm of forgettable slapdash concoctions of fruit juice overwhelmed by sugar.

A new era of complex, nuanced non-alcoholic cocktails gradually emerged, bolstered by the growing proliferation of top-quality NA spirits in liqueurs on the market. These drinks presented new challenges for bartenders, who had to account for the differences in mouthfeel, viscosity, and “burn” between existing alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages. They’ve proven to be deft at clearing these hurdles, and it doesn’t look like they’ll be slowing down any time soon.

2024 – Present: Maximalism Takes Over

All of the trends and innovations to come after craft cocktail revival’s initial educational phase have coalesced into a maximalist movement that almost seems weirdly antithetical to those early days. Over-the-top techniques, theatrical presentations, esoteric ingredients, and decadent cocktail builds that overwhelm the senses and push toward experiential luxury have been in full force, and guests have lapped them up the last couple of years. Bold beverages with brazen builds aren’t exactly new (hello, tiki drinks), but these indulgent expressions feel a bit like a final exam of everything we’ve learned about cocktail evolution in the last 25 years.

Maximalism remains a bona fide trend, but its shelf-life remains to be seen. There’s a chance it could end abruptly. In music terms, the proliferation of maximalist cocktails feels like the height of the progressive rock movement in the early-to-mid 1970s, when 15-minute songs replete with wild time-signature changes, fantastical lyrics, and virtuosic instrumentation took up a healthy chunk of the landscape. The genre (which is interesting and has its merits) was kicked to the curb by the punk rock scene in the late ’70s, which brought rock back to its basic foundations. Perhaps we’ll see a similar phenomenon, where bartenders collectively reject the excesses of maximalism and bring the scene back to its original Milk & Honey-era roots. God only knows, but only time will tell…although there are signs that the time may be now.

content:
Amstel Light may not be terribly popular among today’s beer fans. But it sure could make a great case study for business students.

Once so much a part of pop culture that the New York Times language columnist William Safire wrote a feature about its advertisements, Amstel Light ranked as the No. 1 imported light beer in America for a generation. In the middle of the light beer boom, Amstel Light was credited with teaching millions of Americans that light beer could be flavorful — and maybe even slightly sophisticated.

That cachet earned it an enviable position in East Coast bars of the 1980s and 1990s, says Benj Steinman, president of Beer Marketer’s Insights, a trade publisher for the brewing industry.

“It was a powerhouse brand,” he says. “It was ubiquitous on premise.”

At its apex in 2004, Amstel Light was moving some 10 million cases per year, according to Steinman. But then came slowing sales, with what was once promoted as “the beer drinker’s light beer” shedding 47.7 percent of its volume from 2006 to 2011, a loss that earned the brand a spot on 24/7 Wall St.’s list of “nine beers Americans no longer drink” in 2012.

For industry analysts and insiders, it makes for a cautionary tale, highlighting the importance of consumer preferences, brand focus, and consistent messaging.

Invented for America

Originally, Amstel was a standalone, independent brewery in Amsterdam, named after the Amstel River that flows through the Dutch capital. Founded in 1870, it was once famous for its pilsner, which competed with local rival Heineken until the beer in the iconic green bottle took over Amstel in 1968, after which it turned into one of Heineken’s many sub-brands.

Initially, Amstel Light wasn’t part of that portfolio. But in 1980, Heineken’s U.S. importer, Leo Van Munching, Jr., asked Heineken to send over a light beer. Miller Lite had been given a nationwide rollout in 1975, followed by a massive, hugely influential advertising campaign (“Tastes Great, Less Filling”) and soaring sales that ushered in the light beer era, altering the entire landscape of American brewing. If imported Heineken was meant to compete with standard American lagers, perhaps an imported light beer could compete with Miller Lite, Bud Light, and Coors Light, among others.

“It had a distinctive brand positioning that really resonated with consumers, particularly in northeast urban markets, especially in New York and Boston.”

It might have been about brand differentiation. Or it could have had something to do with the old Heineken-Amstel rivalry that had only ended 12 years earlier. But for whatever reason, when Heineken acquiesced to Van Munching’s request for a light beer import, what arrived was not called “Heineken Light,” but “Amstel Light.” Heineken, the best-selling import in the United States at the time, would remain the full-bodied, full-strength beer, while the Amstel name was used for the company’s light beer segment.

For a while, that approach worked swimmingly. For over a decade, Van Munching & Company owned two enviable slots: the top-selling import, and the most popular imported light beer. It promoted the two brands together, with Heineken and Amstel Light appearing in the same advertisements, using “The Tops in the Field” and “You’re the Tops” taglines. Amstel Light had found its audience.

“It had a distinctive brand positioning that really resonated with consumers, particularly in northeast urban markets, especially in New York and Boston,” Steinman says.

Even outside of the Northeast Corridor, Amstel Light was picking up market share. R.A. Medina spent over 40 years working for a distributor that carried both Heineken and Amstel brands in Central Texas. In that dry, hot region, Amstel Light did very well, especially on tap.

“It actually sold better than Heineken draft,” he says.

Its reputation wasn’t hurt by its brown glass bottles, he recalls, which avoided the characteristic skunkiness associated with Heineken’s green glass.

Following its breakaway success as a U.S. import, Amstel Light was even launched on the Dutch market.

Launching an In-House Rival

It’s impossible to say if there was any internal resentment toward Amstel Light, a brand named after a former rival, among the folks at Heineken, who ended up buying out Van Munching & Company in 1990, with Leo Van Munching staying on until 1993, and renaming it Heineken USA. But just one year after Amstel Light’s best sales ever in 2004, Heineken spent an estimated $50 million promoting a new light beer, Heineken Premium Light, at the start of 2006. (Later, “premium” was dropped from the name.) The New York Times reported on Heineken’s plan to “unleash a barrage of advertising on Web sites,” a newsworthy approach at the time.

“They got a really great running start with Heineken Light,” Steinman says.

That launch — and massive ad spend — meant that Amstel Light wasn’t getting the same attention from the parent company.

“They shifted focus to the brand that had the name on the door,” he says. “The reason why it went down after this is because they introduced Heineken Light.”

Other challenges cropped up around the same time. Dave Williams, president of Bump Williams Consulting, notes that the landscape for imports looked very different during Amstel Light’s salad days of 1980-2004. For nine full years, Amstel Light didn’t have to compete with Corona Light, which first appeared on U.S. shelves in 1989.

“When it was at its highest in the U.S. market, there wasn’t as broad an array of import depth like we see today,” he says.

Of course, there was another big change in American beer around the same time. For a brand that was already positioned as a “trade-up” or “upscale” alternative to mainstream choices, a lot of other options soon started to show up.

“In the early to mid-2000s, craft beer started to take off,” he says. “As the other higher-end offerings in this craft world became viewed as the new elevated alternative to the mainstream choices that were out there in the beer market, it took a hit.”

With the combination of new competition, both in the import sector and in the “upscale alternative” category owned by craft beer, things quickly went off the rails. Look up “Amstel Light” on Google Ngram and what comes back looks like a misshapen letter M, rising straight upward at its launch in 1980, dipping slightly over the next few years before soaring to an even higher second peak in 2004, which slides just a bit in 2005. After that, it drops like a suplex.

For Steinman, Amstel Light could be seen as an example of fixing something that wasn’t broken.

“If there’s any lesson at all I see, they left behind something that was working for them to try something vastly more ambitious that didn’t pan out,” he says. “It ended up that both brands got hurt.”

In fact, the light version of Heineken sank almost as fast as Amstel Light, with sales slipping by 36.7 percent from 2007 to 2012.

The next year, Heineken Premium Light had its own spot on 24/7 Wall St.’s list of “nine beers Americans no longer drink.”

Amstel at Home

That’s not to say all is lost. Despite bad management and marketing missteps, historic Old World breweries often manage to keep some of their mystique and lore. In Amstel’s case, you’re talking about a brand that was originally founded over 150 years ago, and which still maintains a decent customer base in its home country today.

A Dutch data scientist by day who also blogs in English at Tasting Craft Beer, Marcel Haas remembers Amstel from when he first started going out to pubs around Utrecht nearly 30 years ago.

“For me, it was kind of my default beer when I was in a bar,” he says. “It was always considered fine, never perhaps a ‘premium’ choice, but also not a very bad choice. It was just one of the regular brands that bars would have on tap, at least where I grew up.”

In that setting, Amstel obviously wasn’t an import, and it wasn’t seen as particularly fancy or sophisticated. And what Haas remembers is the standard Amstel pilsner, not the designed-for-America light beer.

“They shifted focus to the brand that had the name on the door. The reason why it went down after this is because they introduced Heineken Light.”

“Amstel Light was never big in the Netherlands,” he says. “But it did exist for a while.”

It has since disappeared from the brand’s Dutch-language website, which currently includes a number of similar extensions, including Amstel Bright, Amstel Gold, and Amstel Blonde, all pilsner-ish golden lagers. In the Netherlands, Haas says, Amstel seems to be doing well with its radlers, in both non-alcoholic and low-alcohol (2 percent ABV) variations. Unfortunately, its non-alcoholic beer, Amstel 0.0, sits in the same category (and with a very similar name) as a priority product for its parent company, the top-selling — and heavily promoted — Heineken 0.0.

What beer aficionados like about Amstel, he notes, is something else entirely. At one point, Amstel might have been seen as roughly equal to, or possibly a step down from Heineken, at least in terms of the pilsner style. But when it comes to the strong, malty lagers that the Dutch reach for once the summer ends, Amstel has a solid reputation among connoisseurs.

“Many beer snobs actually do appreciate Amstel Bock,” he says. “Amstel Bock is generally seen as one of the very good Dutch autumn bock beers.”

Those positive associations with the Amstel brand could keep the mystique going, at least until its next moment in the sun. Even in a down market, Williams says, brands still have opportunities to grow. Consumer trends are cyclical, and brands that were once way down can find themselves heading back up again. Some of that is already showing up in the increasing popularity of several Japanese beer brands, as well as once-familiar names like Red Stripe. Heritage lager brands from Europe could be in a prime position to regain customers.

“I think we’ve seen a bit of a reversion back to some of these core styles,” he says. “It’s like we’re out of that era of ‘What’s the hot new thing?’ and it’s more like, ‘What’s the one with provenance? What’s the one with some weight, with some gravitas behind it?”

Among light beers, that used to be Amstel. And perhaps it will be again.

content:
Decades before brands built anticipation for limited-edition drops with countdowns, celebrity appearances, or social media buzz, wine had its own version of the hype cycle. The days may be shorter and the air crisper, but in the world of wine, November is when things start heating up. This is especially true for those who have waited patiently for one of the year’s most anticipated wine events: the release of Beaujolais Nouveau. Made from Gamay grapes grown in the Beaujolais region of France, these light, fruit-forward wines are released annually on the third Thursday of November to international fanfare.

Beaujolais Nouveau began as a local harvest tradition, made to be celebrated within weeks after the grapes are picked, not months or years. In the 1950s and ’60s, the release became a sort of race to market, with négociants and couriers competing to get the first bottles from Beaujolais to Parisian restaurants and bistros. In one famous marketing stunt, a tuxedoed waiter parachuted into the city of lights and landed at the base of the Eiffel Tower with one of the newest bottlings in hand.

In 1985, the Institut National de l’Origine et de la Qualité (INAO), France’s official appellation authority, standardized the release date to exactly 12:01 a.m. on the third Thursday of November. This midnight drop is now celebrated from Japan to New York City and beyond, giving wine drinkers around the world a shared occasion to savor the year’s Gamay harvest.

The Man Behind the Hype

Few understood the potential of “limited-edition” better than Georges Duboeuf. Dubbed pape du Beaujolais (the pope of Beaujolais), Duboeuf was born into a humble family of winegrowers and later founded his eponymous négociant house in 1964. Rising to become one of Beaujolais’s great ambassadors, he often hand-delivered bottles to celebrated Michelin chefs by bicycle, helping transform Nouveau from a sleepy local harvest celebration into an international phenomenon. As he traveled extensively to promote the wines and build relationships with growers across the region, he popularized the now-famous rallying cry, “Le Beaujolais Nouveau est arrivé!” Or, “The Beaujolais Nouveau has arrived!” 

Duboeuf also understood the power of spectacle decades before TikTok influencers and digital marketing teams. He ensured that bottles of Nouveau were often rushed around the world by plane, including on the legendary (though sadly now decommissioned) Concorde back in the day. In 1988, he gave the term “publicity stunt” new meaning when actor James Coburn, known for his powderkeg acting in movie fight scenes, famously led a midnight departure of trucks from the Duboeuf winery on horseback, bottles of the new vintage in tow. 

The brand’s striking flowered labels became a calling card for the annual release, making Georges Duboeuf Beaujolais Nouveau as recognizable on restaurant tables and retail shelves as the fanfare surrounding its arrival. The line has also stayed fresh through one-off collaborations with top creators in its annual Artist Collector Series, working with independent artists like Felice Kite, Maeve Croghan, Laura Runge, and Chloe Meyer (among others) to reinvent the label’s iconic fleur through fresh interpretations and vivid, original illustrations. The result is a bottle that gives a sense of being both timeless and new, bringing a fresh burst of creativity to a tradition built around celebrating the moment.

Why a Wine Released Just Weeks After Harvest Still Fascinates Wine Drinkers

All the hype wouldn’t have lasted if the wines weren’t an experience in themselves. After hand-harvesting the Gamay grapes, the wine can go from vine to bottle in roughly six to eight weeks using a technique known as carbonic maceration that produces an intensely fresh, aromatic red wine. This light-bodied, juicy style is naturally low in tannins and ABV, with bright acidity, and notes of raspberry and cherry fruit, while some fans covet hints of ripe banana and even bubblegum candy.  

While many styles of wine are built for the patience of cellar aging, Nouveau is built for the here and now, and is best enjoyed within a short time after release. Luckily for American drinkers, Beaujolais Nouveau Day falls just before Thanksgiving, making the style a natural guest at the holiday table. Its bright acidity cuts through rich foods, while its fresh, fruity profile pairs easily with turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, and roasted vegetables. Served with a slight chill, it is equally at home alongside a charcuterie board as it is with the main course.

Honoring the Past, Toasting to Tomorrow

Decades ahead of the curve, before long lines for the latest culinary fads or members-only tastings, Beaujolais Nouveau was already poised to create a singular sensory event built on anticipation, timing, and more than a little theatricality. The annual release has become a much-beloved tradition, and a delightful reason to celebrate and gather. So this holiday season, bring a famously glamorous guest to the dinner table – a bottle of Georges Duboeuf Beaujolais Nouveau — fresh off the presses.

This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on household spending on alcohol in the U.S., the EU’s approval of Chianti rosé, the latest product releases, and more.

News to know:

  • Average U.S. household spending on alcohol hits record low: Alcohol purchases comprised a 0.77 percent share of the average U.S. household spending last year, a record low and 2 percent year-over-year drop, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Consumer Expenditure Survey. The average American household spent $630 on booze in 2025, down from $643 the previous year.
  • EU approves Chianti rosé distinction, other landmark amendments: Pink wine will now be a recognized category in Chianti, Tuscany’s largest and most popular wine sub-region. The European Union approved the distinction as part of a total overhaul of Chianti’s wine production regulations, which also lowered the minimum amount of Sangiovese to be considered a Chianti blend.
  • National Wine and Spirits (NWS) challenges $6.6 million payment to RNDC’s parent company: NWS filed a complaint against RNDC last week to prevent it from paying $6.57 million to its parent company. NWS and RNDC were previously in a joint venture for Kentucky’s liquor distribution business before selling it to KEG 1 Kentucky after RNDC’s fallout. As part of the plan, a portion of the money from that sale, roughly $6.6 million, was set to go to RNDC’s parent company to offset debts. NWS is arguing that RDNC damaged the joint venture and that NWS is entitled to a portion of the buyout.
  • Sazerac’s bullish shopping spree shows no signs of slowing: The Louisville, Ky.-based spirits juggernaut bought Oregon craft brewery Full Sail Brewing for an undisclosed sum and launched a $605 million project to expand four of its Kentucky distilleries. These advancements come in the same year as Sazerac’s pickups of ready-to-drink brands Dirty Shirley and Au Vodka, as well as its $15 billion attempt at scooping Brown-Forman.
  • DoorDash agreed to buy Instacart for $17 billion: The landmark deal, announced last Thursday, will loop the U.S.’s largest grocery delivery app under the same umbrella as the country’s biggest takeout service. The transaction values Instacart shares at $65 each.

Product releases to watch:

  • The Macallan releases the final iteration of special New Years Eve series: The Macallan is closing out A Night on Earth, an annual series geared toward celebrating different cultures’ New Years Eve celebrations, with a limited-edition single malt. The Finale, the collection’s fifth installment, honors New Orleans and is available online and at The Macallan Estate Boutique for a suggested retail price of $125.
  • WhistlePig gets indulgent with dessert-like rye: WhistlePig is debuting 12-Year Single Finish Maple Crème Brûlée Rye, a whiskey inspired by wintry, holiday flavors. The limited-edition rye aged in the brand’s ex-maple syrup barrels, which were charred to mimic the burnt sugar flavors of crème brûlée. WhistlePig’s Maple Crème Brûlée is now available online and at select retailers, bars, and restaurants for a suggested price of $124.99.
  • Tears of Llorona debuts a five-year-old extra añejo: The premium Jalisco tequila brand is releasing its latest small-batch extra añejo later this month. Hills of Los Altos aged for five years — two years over the minimum — and will be available in limited quantities for a suggested retail price of $279.99.

content:
I recently somehow added Google Discover to my iPhone and suddenly I was getting push notifications for content it thought I might like to read. It was annoying at first, but I had to admit the picks were usually spot-on with my interests.

Hosannas to Michael Olise’s latest stunning performance in the Champions League.

Critical reviews of “You Can See Everything.”

Reviews for the new Georgian restaurant in my neighborhood.

And one morning a few weeks ago, I got pushed a just-published Tasting Table story entitled: I Tried 11 Cheap Beers And Ranked Them Worst To Best

I didn’t need to know who wrote it. I didn’t even need to read it yet. I knew it would be a viral hit.

Indeed, within days the article would be widely shared on social media and message boards and syndicated by Yahoo Life and AOL. (For what it’s worth, author Julia Duda would select Miller High Life for “its impeccable balance between crispness and flavor.”)

Now entering its fourth decade of existence, the “cheap beers ranked” listicle is seemingly, still, one of the most reliable ways for a publication to garner easy viral traffic.

Consuming Reports

June 1996. Consumer Reports, that ad-free arbiter of car, appliance, and electronics quality, decided to, for the first time, put its powers of evaluation toward “mass-marketed beers.” They gathered 17 academically-trained beer tasters (brewmasters and PhDs in fermentation sciences mainly) to determine the “blue-collar bargain of the beer cooler” by tasting 69 different beers.

The winner was Old Milwaukee, then the second cheapest beer in the country, averaging $1.69 per 6-pack. Second place was even more surprising — Stroh’s, created by German immigrants in 1850, and not even a top 25 best-selling beer in America by 1996. Third place got even stranger, being awarded to Red Dog, a now-defunct product from Miller.

Even in this mid-1990s nascent era of craft beer and online chatter, the unexpected results went viral — print viral.

The Washington Post covered it, quite aghast at the report and with a ton of editorializing from writer Marc Fisher. “[The result] makes sense — if the Old Milwaukee had been delivered to the tasters by Learjet, while competitors’ brews were placed in blinding sunlight for several years.”

The article was covered by The New York Times, the Los Angeles Times, and Tampa Bay Times. AP business writer Brian S. Akre asked “Could it be that Bud’s been dethroned as the King of Beers?” While the New York Daily News thought “Magazine Ratings are Hard to Swallow” and gathered 25 of their own employees to conduct their own tasting.

Though surely earnest in their intentions, Consumer Reports had unwittingly taught the mainstream media that rating cheap beers could inspire such intense debate that virality was all but guaranteed. The race was on, and for the next 30 years “cheap beers ranked” has been as dependable an article as one can publish.

The Best Worst

These listicles would mostly remain the purview of print for the first decade of the 21st century. The Washington Post would do their own cheap beer blind taste test in 2009, defining that as ones priced at less than $6 a sixer. Baltimore’s beloved local lager National Bohemian would win and the story would be covered by NPR and others.

It would take modern internet culture — and the rise of high-priced craft beer — however, to launch “cheap beers ranked” into the stratosphere. Audiences have all but demanded this story.

In 2012, Slate offered its readers a chance to assign a feature to one of its authors. The top seven picks — which included “Make Seth Stevenson explain the scourge of scaffolding” and “Make Matt Yglesias explain why hotel rooms cost so much” — were voted on, and ultimately the winner was “Make Troy Patterson review cheap beers.”

His resulting article, “The Best Worst Brews,” didn’t really rank beers but just had him trying and offering his thoughts on some cheap notables like Natural Light (“If you’re having only one beer, Natty Light is one to avoid.”). Perhaps due to his wishy-washy thoughts and lack of a forced ranking, the story only received one comment and, so far as I can tell, is just about the only cheap beers ranked listicle to not go viral. Maybe Slate should have opted for that Yglesias story.

In 2013, just as craft beer was undergoing a massive boom and clearly differentiating itself from the macros, offbeat sports blog Deadspin, then at the peak of its powers, offered “36 Cheap American Beers, Ranked.”

Author Will Gordon would stir debate by blasting beloved favorites like Miller High Life and Yuengling while crowning Minnesota’s Grain Belt Premium as his No. 1. As I’ve written about before, this was an era where you could go insanely viral on the internet and this piece did massive numbers, with over 2 million views, thousands of comments on the article itself, and a colossal amount of sharing it across the World Wide Web. Gordon appeared on AM radio and podcasts to discuss it and CBS News even did a report on it.

It ended up being Deadspin’s 7th most popular post of the year — in a year they uncovered the Manti Te’o dead girlfriend hoax — and might very well be the most widely-read piece of beer criticism ever written.

So seismic was Gordon’s article that other websites tried to quickly draft off the traffic, like First We Feast, which posted “America’s Best Cheap Beers, Ranked” a mere day later, even addressing its inspiration.

“Yesterday, writer Will Gordon set a certain segment of the suds-swilling, butt-scratching Internet on fire,” wrote then-editor-in-chief of First We Feast (and future “Hot Ones” creator) Chris Schonberger. “Since we’d been working on our own cheap-beer rankings in honor of July 4, our first thought was, ‘Damn, we’ve been scooped!’, followed shortly by, Oh wait, this is not an original idea at all!’, and then finally — upon reading through Gordon’s hastily summarized picks — ‘This list completely blows!’”

Schonberger would end up ranking Narragansett Lager as his No. 1, which incidentally Gordon had already ranked as his No. 2.

I think Gordon’s article was such a hit because he went above and beyond everyone else who had ever done it before, ranking 36 different beers, including plenty of beloved local lagers like Iron City, Olympia, Rainier, and Lone Star, while not being afraid to take down sacred cows. There was something for literally everyone to applaud — or be pissed off about — in an era where Twitter was likewise at its zenith and everybody had something to say and post.

Even Gordon, who would offer rebuttal to himself the very next year when he published for Deadspin a mea culpa that “Schlitz Is America’s Best Cheap Beer.” He had previously ranked it No. 30.

From Awful to Drinkable

You would think that would be the end of it, but no, the cheap beers listicle would storm on into the second half of the decade.

The Washington Post yet again went to the well in 2016, keying in on canned beers sold in D.C. bars for $4 or less. New York’s Genesee Cream Ale would prevail. A website called Cheapism would do their own rankings in 2016, considering anything $10 or less per 6-pack.

And, yes, of course, we here at VinePair have done it too, with two separate cheap beer lists penned in 2017 alone. There was “8 Cheap Light Beers, Ranked” (the little discussed Bud Light Platinum won), and the “11 Cheap American Beers Ranked From Awful to Drinkable” (or Natural Ice to Narragansett) which reeled in a cool 1.2 million views.

Over the last decade, cheap beers have been ranked by Maxim, Gear Patrol, Uproxx, Delish, Paste, Outside, Taste of Home, Wide Open Country, The Takeout, and Porch Drinking.

We haven’t even discussed the countless free alt-weeklies, college newspapers, personal blogs, message boards, and YouTube videos (8 million views!) offering their own rankings.

And here we are in 2026, an era where the cheap beers listicle improbably still prevails. Things have changed, though, and the lists have likewise changed with the times.

If those initial lists two and three decades ago mostly only included multinational-owned American adjunct lagers, slowly but surely cheap Mexican lagers started appearing as well — matching the rise of the category itself — as did so-called “supermarket craft beers” like Brooklyn Lager, which took the top spot when Food & Wine published We Ranked 20 Mass-Market North American Lagers by Taste Alone — Here’s Who Won just this June. (For what it’s worth, Brooklyn Lager was actually one of the more expensive pints one could buy when I first moved to New York in 2000.)

More importantly, and perhaps as the authors of these articles have shifted from jaded Gen X writers to Millennials and now Zoomers, the idea of these lists as ironic counterpoints to the rise of craft beer has begun to fade and most publications are now publishing these listicles more earnestly. Like Chowhound, who in July offered Ranking Cheap Beer Brands From The Least Drinkable To The Absolute Best. Author Sarah Dealy noted that these beers are “near and dear to my heart,” even going on to explain that she’s never been a fan of expensive double IPAs that cost $9 a pint. She, like Duda at Tasting Table, opted for Miller High Life as her No. 1.

Cheap Cheep

Beer, like life, is only getting more expensive.

People are losing interest in craft beer and that old “macro vs. craft” war is all but over.

But everyone still has their own opinion on and, theoretically, can afford cheap beer. Perhaps that’s why once-maligned, low-brow brands like Busch Light are all of a sudden booming in sales. People can’t afford to be snarky toward swill any more. Likewise, a cheap beer listicle might be the least expensive piece of tasting content a food or drink publication can produce.

It’s easy to tell a just-out-of-college freelancer to go review 10 macro beers — they’ll have already tasted most and already formed an opinion on plenty. It would be harder to get them to assess the best papalote mezcals on the market. And, as the spirits editor here, I’m sad to admit that also would get a lot less traffic as I doubt most people have had or have strong thoughts on, say, the Sanzekan Papalote ‘Eufemio Sanchez.’

The cheap beer listicle is an idea that has outlived print, personal blogs, message board culture, Twitter, and Deadspin (now owned by a digital media company in Malta!), and is now basically the last evergreen feature that will surely outlive us all. The next incarnation of these lists will probably be written by AI agents, but it doesn’t take a supercomputer to know how to reel readers in. You just need the headline.

In fact, just yesterday as I write this, Google Discover pushed me yet another story entitled “The Hands-Down Best Cheap Beer Isn’t Pabst Blue Ribbon or Miller Lite.”

I couldn’t help myself. I clicked.

content:
The tradition of snacking on something salty, cheesy, or nutty while imbibing at a local bar can be traced back centuries. And still today, drinkers just can’t resist having a bowl of peanuts or potato chips to accompany a crisp pint of beer after a work day or a dish of olives with an afternoon spritz. But beyond these classic small bites, each corner of the world has developed a certain set of bar snacks that go along with its particular drinking culture. For some countries this means bites of cheese-filled fritters between sips of a local brew, while others lean lighter with easygoing seafood dishes to complement bright, crisp wines.

These distinct snacks can be seen at watering holes across the globe, and in some places, like New York City, you can experience a world of bar snacks in one afternoon: from the spice bag at Bar Snack in the East Village to the pork scratchings at the West Village’s own British pub, Dean’s. While New Yorkers are lucky to have easy access to just about any world cuisine at establishments around the city, these bar snacks have interesting origin stories of their own.

No matter what you snack on when knocking back a cold one, it’s important — if not enriching — to understand the cultural ties of those dishes. From the spice-laced peanuts of Mexico and China to deep-fried balls of meat from Western Europe, here are the most popular bar snacks around the world.

Europe

Italy

Stuzzichini

You can almost always expect small ramekins of salty and appetite-whetting snacks to arrive alongside each round of Aperol Spritzes, Negronis, Garibaldis, and the like on cocktail-hour tables across Italy. The northwest city of Turin was the birthplace of the tradition of the Italian aperitivo hour, where the 18th-century advent of vermouth sparked a ritual of pre-dinner, low-ABV drinks and small bites. Stuzzichini are the small, usually savory snacks served during aperitivo hour. The customary mix of small dishes might include taralli — ring-shaped, baked crackers that either come plain or flavored with herbs — olives, peanuts, or even potato chips.

United Kingdom

Scotch Eggs

Coming from the U.K. — where pub culture involves hefty beers and hearty snacks to match — is the Scotch egg. The dish is a hard- or soft-boiled egg wrapped in sausage meat, coated in breadcrumbs, and fried. While its name suggests it originated in Scotland, most food historians believe English cooks first invented the Scotch egg in the 18th century. (One retail store in London claims to have been among the first to make the dish in 1738). Some accounts also theorize that Scotch eggs emerged as a result of the transfer of cultures between the U.K. and India via the East India Company. Those claims say Scotch eggs were a British take on Nargisi Kofta, a traditional Indian dish of a similar format, with a cooked egg encased in spiced ground meat.

Pork Scratchings

Pork scratchings are slices of pig skin that are dehydrated and fried until they puff into an airy, crackingly crisp texture. Already rich in meaty and umami flavors, pork scratchings are often seasoned with just a dash of salt. What differentiates scratchings from “rinds” or “cracklings” is that they usually come from the skin on the pig’s hind legs. Similar to Scotch eggs, the rich, deep-fried flavor of pork scratchings serves to complement the heavy profile of pub-style brews. They first came about among impoverished communities in 1800s England, where people used every last bit of the livestock for a cheap, filling snack. Today, pork snatchings are often sold in retail stores packaged in bags or served fresh at pubs.

Germany

Pretzels

No, German pretzels aren’t just an Instagrammable fad for tourists to pose with while in their lederhosen at Munich’s biergartens. The snack dates back to the Middle Ages, and some historians think an Italian monk was the first to tie a simple dough into a knot as a symbol of the Christian Holy Trinity. In the 1100s, the tradition then spread to what is now Germany, when the famous shape of the knotted bread became the go-to signage for bakeries. Today, the salted snack is served at bars around the world. In Germany, pretzels are most often soft and can be an accompaniment to beers served in mugs or steins.

Spain

Gildas

Gildas come from Spain’s Basque Country — the stretch of land between northeast Spain and southwest France, where the cuisine is centered around seafood and small bites. The handheld snack is presented on a small skewer, with bites alternating between green olives, pickled hot peppers, and anchovies cured in oil. While now ubiquitous around Spain and at Basque-inspired restaurants around the world, Gildas didn’t come about until the 20th century: San Sebastián’s Bar Casa Vallés first introduced the dish in 1946 after a regular customer skewered the three ingredients together and consumed the ensemble as one. Some snackers like to take each element individually, whereas others eat them in the same bite. No matter how you go at it, gildas bring strong, piquant flavors of brine, vinegar, and spice and commonly accompany a glass of Txakoli or vermouth — two popular choices at Spanish bars.

Croquetas

Croquetas are now most common at Spanish tapas bars and restaurants, but the French were the first to shape leftover meat scraps — and eventually béchamel — into a ball to then bread and fry them. But it wasn’t until the Spanish adopted the dish in the 1800s that it became as popular around the world as it is today. On tapas menus, croquetas take many different forms. Most traditional are the croquetas de jamón, but bargoers can also find examples with chicken, cod, or cheese.. Croquetas are particularly popular in Catalonia, where light, sessionable beers like Estrella Damm or bottles of bubbly Cava are common for washing down the heavy snack.

Ireland

Spice Bag

Consumed as both late-night street food and a pub snack alongside a Guinness, spice bags are one of Ireland’s latest claims to fame. While the name doesn’t reveal much about what’s inside, it refers to a mixture of crispy fried chicken, french fries, peppers, and onions all haphazardly thrown into a bag, doused in dry spices, and shaken together. At its core, spice bags are a blend of Irish pub food and Chinese flavors: Most accounts say Sunflower Chinese, a takeout spot in Dublin, invented the now-popular snack in 2006. Some may say spice bags are best when eaten after a few pints to satiate your appetite, but the balance of a spicy kick with the toasted, chocolatey notes of Guinness is some great craic.

The Netherlands

Bitterballen

Similar to croquetas, bitterballen are deep fried orbs with a crisp, craggly breadcrumb exterior that gives way to a creamy, meaty filling. Traditional recipes combine a roux with chunks of cooked meat — usually beef — and its juices to create an incredibly rich, velvety mouthfeel. While their exact origin is unknown, bitterballen are believed to have emerged during the 1600s. Now common at traditional bars in Amsterdam and across the Netherlands, the snack is usually dipped in a bright, spicy mustard to cut through the unctuous flavors. Bitterballan also accompany crisp Dutch lagers like Amstel or Heineken.

North America

United States

Chicken Wings

Whether at a dive, sports, or a regular neighborhood bar in the U.S., you can bet chicken wings will be on the menu. The spicy, bright orange Buffalo sauce may be the most common to dress chicken wings, but with the Buffalo wing’s ubiquity came the expansion of options, with lemon-pepper, barbecue, and garlic-parmesan sauces now popular on menus. On the side usually comes a ramekin of ranch or bleu cheese dressing and spears of celery and carrots to cut through the spicy, salty, and fatty elements. Chicken wings became so beloved within the American consumer consciousness that national and international chains like Buffalo Wild Wings and Wing Stop have become a go-to. Chicken wings are often relegated to more laid-back establishments like dives or sports bars and often consumed with light beers — though, they arguably go with anything.

Nachos

Nachos originated in Mexico, not far from the Texas border. And while the dish — a heaping pile of tortilla chips most commonly covered in toppings like queso, beans, meat, and jalapeños — is still popular in its home country, the U.S. has taken it in as its own. Relatively easy to execute and share among a table of people, nachos are the ultimate communal dish to enjoy alongside a few Margaritas.

Mexico

Cacahuates Botaneros

Originating from the southern Mexico region of Oaxaca, “cacahuates botaneros” roughly translates to “bar snack peanuts.” You can find the snack at the center of a table of cervezas, micheladas, Margaritas, or Palomas. The dish traditionally mixes peanuts with a number of seasonings, such as garlic, chilis, oil, salt, and lime juice, before toasting the ensemble over a stove. A halved lime usually comes beside a bowl of the nuts to brighten everything up.

Asia

Korea

Corn Cheese

Corn cheese, known locally as kon-chijeu, is a Korean dip that’s exactly as it sounds: a warm mix of corn and melted cheese. A combination of the corn, mozzarella, mayonnaise, and other ingredients is baked in a skillet and, immediately after removing from the oven, topped with slices of scallions or chives and served sizzling hot. It first gained popularity around the late 20th century, but it is now a common food to snack on while drinking in South Korea. Corn cheese is one of the many dishes in the “anju” category — a suite of modern Korean drinking snacks that also includes fried chicken, shredded squid, and blood sausage.

China

Drunken Peanuts

Coming from the Szechuan region in China — an area beloved for a cuisine that often features a numbing peppercorn spice — drunken peanuts (also known as jiǔguǐ huāshēng) got their name from being a popular snack at bars, where they are usually consumed with beer. The peanuts are either fried or roasted before getting the mala seasoning treatment, which is a blend of red chili peppers and Szechuan peppercorns. There’s little account of drunken peanuts’ origins other than their long ties to Szechuan cuisine, but in recent years, the snack has commercialized, with a number of companies packaging the peanuts to be sold in retail stores.

Japan

Chicken Karaage

A popular dish at Japanese izakaya bars, chicken Karaage is a crispy, crunchy snack of fried chicken to enjoy with an ice cold Asahi or crisp Toki highball. It’s made by frying up small pieces of thigh meat marinated in a ginger, soy sauce, and garlic dressing. The dish actually has origins in China, where deep frying bite-sized foods was first common and then brought to Japan. It especially spread around Japan after World War II, when food became sparse and frying pieces of chicken became a cheap alternative for a satiating meal.

South America

Brazil

Coxinha

Coxinhas are fried, cone-shaped bites filled with chicken with spices, onions, garlic, and cheese. There are a number of theories about the origins of the dish — some involve Brazilian royalty, and others say it was a natural extension of French croquettes. The word “coxhina” translates to “little thigh” in Portuguese, which some say is a nod to the fried dish’s teardrop-like appearance that is made to resemble the drumstick of a chicken. Both a street food and a bar snack, coxinhas are served with light, easy-drinking beers.
